headline: Programmers are the easiest profession for AI to replace, easier than truck drivers
summary: Unlike other professions, programming's text-in, text-out nature makes it uniquely vulnerable to AI automation, leading to significant workforce reductions even in profitable companies.
details: Programming is uniquely susceptible to AI automation because its input and output are text, and evaluation is machine-checked code execution. This makes it a perfect task for language models, unlike professions with physical or human interaction barriers.

One product manager used Claude to generate a feature spec and code in 90 seconds, bypassing experienced engineers. The role shifted from building to justifying why a human should build it, highlighting a fundamental change in job function.

Companies are prioritizing cost efficiency over marginal quality improvements. The market values 85% accuracy at $0.03 per query more than 100% accuracy at a $150,000 annual salary, making human programmers less competitive.
Snap Inc. laid off 1,000 engineers (16% of its workforce) after stating 65% of its code is AI-generated. The company's stock rose 11% the same day, rewarding the cost-cutting measure.

Atlassian, makers of Jira, also laid off 1,600 people, including over 900 engineering roles, despite being profitable with 26% revenue growth. This signals that companies are reducing engineering staff because they simply don't need as many.

OpenAI's own 'Harness Engineering' team, comprising 3-7 engineers, generated roughly one million lines of code in five months using Codex. These engineers primarily reviewed AI-generated code, effectively becoming QA for an AI.

Historically, professions were replaced by external forces. Programmers, however, are building the very AI tools that are making them obsolete. This unprecedented situation means they are forging the 'guillotine' for their own roles.

headline_marked: [[AI Slop Detector Flagged My Own Writing]] — A developer's surprising self-audit
headline: AI Slop Detector Flagged My Own Writing — A developer's surprising self-audit
summary: A new AI slop detector, kill-ai-slop, identified generic, machine-like patterns in a human author's articles, revealing subtle "AI-generated" tells in their own writing.
details: A developer tested kill-ai-slop, a new AI content detector, against their own articles. To their surprise, the tool flagged several instances of "AI-generated" patterns in their human-written content. This challenged their perception of their unique writing voice.

The kill-ai-slop project by yetone is a Node.js Agent Skill for tools like Claude Code or Cursor. It features a 23-point checklist and a multilingual field guide with before-and-after examples, designed to identify patterns that make content look and read machine-made.

The skill scans HTML, CSS, and copy for code-level signals, sentence structures, and design elements associated with AI-generated "slop." It reports, triages, and proposes fixes without editing files directly, and is dependency-free.

The project stands out for its well-researched catalog and specific explanations, practicing what it preaches with a deliberately sparse, "paper-and-ink" website design. It avoids gradients, emojis, and uses a single editorial red for emphasis, mirroring a proofreader's pen.

The 23 "tells" are categorized into six groups: Colour, Type, Copy, Components, Layout, and "Evolved Slop" for newer, less obvious patterns. Each tell includes a detection pattern, an explanation of why it reads as machine-made, and a suggested fix.

The author's self-audit focused on the "Copy" section, revealing patterns like the "not just X — it's Y" introductory frame in their first article. This structure, designed to sound insightful, often delivers vague contrasts, making it sound like a generated page template.

Other flagged patterns included the use of "→" as a visual separator, which functions like an emoji by borrowing visual weight instead of earning it through writing. The author also admitted to using bolding more than strictly necessary, a mild hit on the "when every emphasized word isn't, none is" principle.

The detector found that technical sections with specific details like curl commands or API responses were generally "slop-free." These sections impose a concrete structure that prevents vague language, making them harder for AI to generate convincingly.

Conversely, the "slop patterns" were concentrated in transitional paragraphs and bridge sentences, such as "This is useful because..." or "What I found was...". These mechanical connectors often lack substance and are easily generated, highlighting where human writing can unintentionally mimic AI.
